newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova expects to resume growth in 1997. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Moldova expects to resume growth in 1997. [CORRECTED 13:45 GMT]

text.p: Moldova's government expects the economy to grow in 1997 for the first time after five years of recession, a senior minister said.
"Our primary goal for the next year is to maintain macroeconomic stabilisation and to restore growth," Ion Gutu, Moldovan Deputy Prime Minister, told a news conference late on Wednesday.
The new government, formed after December's parliamentary elections, has set ambitious targets for 1997.
It is planning increases in gross domestic product of 5-7 percent, industrial production of 11 percent, agriculture of 6.3 percent and exports of 5 percent.
The programme stipulates a further reduction in inflation to 10-13 percent and a narrowing of the budget deficit to three percent of GDP.
International financial organisations have praised Moldova for its reform record, saying it is one of the most successful former Soviet countries in terms of macroeconomic stabilisation.
The Moldovan leu has been stable since its introduction in 1993, and inflation slowed to 15.1 percent last year from 105 percent in 1994.
But in terms of structural reforms Moldova is substantially behind the Baltic states, foreign donors say.
"We did not fulfil all the measures agreed upon with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank," Gutu said.

In 1996 the government failed to end the decline in the economy. Instead of expected growth, GDP contracted by eight percent and the budget deficit was eight percent of GDP instead of the planned 3.5 percent.
The government's most urgent tasks are to pay off pension and salaries arrears, which now amount to 400 million lei, and to curb crime and corruption, Gutu said.
The government will focus on privatising companies for cash rather than for free vouchers, concentrating on the energy sector and telecommunications.
It will introduce laws making it possible to sell, buy and mortgage the land.
The government intends to increase energy tariffs by 35 percent for households and 10-15 percent for companies by the end of the year, and earlier this week raised bread prices by 17 percent.
It has prepared a bill increasing the pension age to 60 from 55 for women and to 65 from 60 years for men. But the trade unions and the parliament oppose this legislation.
